https://telex.hu/g7/vallalat/2026/08/01/.text: Menü Kereső Legendás magyar gyár kerül ismét hazai tulajdonba Vállalat A Vajda-Papír Kft. dunaföldvári üzeme 2026. január 20-án – Fotó: Máthé Zoltán / MTI Szabó Milán Jóváhagyta a Gazdasági Versenyhivatal , hogy a Vajda Papír Kft. felvásárolja a Sofidel Hungary Kft. saját márkás háztartási papírtermékgyártási és részbeni értékesítési üzletágát, annak lábatlani gyárával együtt. Így az ottani, nagy hagyományú papírgyártás évtizedes multi háttér után hamarosan ismét magyar tulajdonban működik majd. Előzmények: Lábatlanon már az előző század elején is gyártottak papírt, a tevékenység modernebb formájában az 1960-as években indult el. Az üzem a privatizáció során görög tulajdonba került, de a magyarországi cég a 2008-as válságban bedőlt, a gyárat pedig később lebontották . A lábatlani papírgyártás Bodrogai Ferencnek köszönhetően maradt fenn, aki a privatizáció után távozott a papírgyárból, és megalapította saját cégét, a Forest Papírt, amely az ezredfordulótól kezdve szintén Lábatlanon termelt. Ennek lakossági üzletágát 2016-ban adta el az olasz Sofidelnek, ezt veszi meg most a Vajda Papír. Miért fontos ez? A Vajda Papír azon kevés magyarországi vállalkozás közé tartozik, amely családi vállalkozásból nagyvállalattá tudott fejlődni, és megvetette lábát a nemzetközi piacon. A vállalat már külföldi gyártókapacitással is rendelkezik, és sikerét jelzi, hogy egy olasz multinacionális cég – mintegy 160 fős * Ez a Sofidel Hungary teljes létszáma, de szinte mindenki átkerülhet a Vajda Papírhoz az alapján, hogy áprilisban Vajda Attila 170 fős létszámot említett a lábatlani gyár kapcsán. – üzletágát tudta megvásárolni, miközben sokkal gyakoribbak a fordított irányú tranzakciók a magyar gazdaságban. Mit mondanak ők? „A tranzakció lezárását követően minden kollégára számítunk, és további létszámbővítést is tervezünk. A lábatlani dolgozók számára is elérhetővé válnak a Vajda Papír-csoportnál megszokott juttatások, képzési lehetőségek és hosszú távú karrierút” – mondta Vajda Attila, a csoport alapító tulajdonos-ügyvezetője. Alulnézet: az 1999-ben alapított Vajda Papír 2011-ben kezdte meg a nagyvállalati struktúrára való átállást, és ebben az évben vezette be a hazai és külföldi piacra szóló márkája, az Ooops! forgalmazását. Norvégiában is vett gyártósort a vállalat 2013-ban, az induláskor száz alkalmazottal, így már nemcsak exporttal, de gyártókapacitással is megjelent a nemzetközi piacon. Zöldmezős beruházást hajtottak végre 2018-ban Dunaföldváron, ami lehetővé tette, hogy itthon is képes legyen a vállalat alappapír gyártásra a szintén száz alkalmazottal induló gyárban. Duális képzőhelyi megállapodást kötött 2020-ben a vállalat, hozzájárulva ahhoz, hogy két évtizedet követően újraindult a nappali tagozatos papíripari és feldolgozói szakképzés. 11 milliárd forint értékben bocsátott ki kötvényt a cég a Magyar Nemzeti Bank Növekedési Kötvényprogramja keretében 2021-ben. 2023 és 2026 között közel 119 milliárd értékű befektetésekhez kapott majdnem 43 milliárd forint vissza nem térítendő állami támogatást. Legutóbb idén januárban kapott a dunaföldvári üzem 70,8 milliárd forintos kapacitásbővítéséhez 24,9 milliárd vissza nem térítendő támogatást a vállalat. Ez volt idén a legnagyobb beruházástámogatási összeg. Számokban: 2021 óta nő a vállalat árbevétele, 2024-ig közel háromszorosára bővült. A tavalyi számait még nem tette közzé a vállalat. A legutóbbi két ismert év számottevő nyereséget hozott, veszteséggel utoljára 2022-ben zártak, amikor tízmilliárd forintot költöttek gép- és technológiai beruházásra. A bevételi adatok alapján látszik, hogy egyre fontosabb a nemzetközi piac a cég számára. A konszolidált, tehát a teljes vállalatcsoport adatait tartalmazó mutató szerint 2024-ben az export már több mint 50 százalékkal felülmúlta a hazai árbevételt. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4v.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pirates manage to board ships operating a long way from the coast and then guide them closer to the shore By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent Published 13 minutes ago A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran. Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates. It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade. "Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity." That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north. Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz. And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping. "I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast. Image source, VesselFinder Image caption, The MV Lutuf, seen here near the Turkish port of GÃ¼llÃ¼k last year, was hijacked on 17 August Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf. The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences. Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons. The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned. That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage. A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024. But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them. Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland. And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload. The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative. "You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity. "And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well." He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast. But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions. "I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says. Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings. Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Fishing by international trawlers off Puntland's coast has had an impact on this vital local industry (file photo) The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify. "There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital. He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday. "The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more." Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes. Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them. Puntland authorities have been more outspoken. Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast. The BBC has not independently verified his allegations. The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operationâ¦ in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out. Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say. There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed. https://ct24.ceskatelevize.cz/clanek/dom.text: Ve věku sto let zemřel válečný veterán a plukovník ve výslužbě Josef Turek, poslední v Česku pobývající československý voják, který se za druhé světové války zúčastnil bojů u francouzského přístavu Dunkerk. O jeho úmrtí informoval odbor válečných veteránů a válečných hrobů ministerstva obrany na síti X. Letos v únoru Turek obdržel francouzský Řád čestné legie V. stupně. Turek byl v roce 1944 povolán do německé armády a nasazen na západní frontě ve Francii. Po zajetí americkými vojáky se dostal do Velké Británie, kde vstoupil do československé zahraniční armády. Jako tankista Československé samostatné obrněné brigády se následně zapojil do bojů u Dunkerku, které trvaly do konce druhé světové války. Když se po demobilizaci vrátil domů, jeho blízcí byli překvapeni, protože ho považovali za mrtvého. Na tuto událost vzpomínal jeho syn Josef Turek mladší v rozhovoru zveřejněném ministerstvem obrany. Kvůli své válečné minulosti a službě v československých jednotkách na západní frontě strávil Turek většinu profesního života jako dělník. Po návratu do Československa působil krátce jako instruktor řidičů tanků, později pracoval u železnice. Poslední roky života pobýval ve Středisku komplexní péče o veterány ve Vojenské nemocnici v Olomouci. Za účast v bojích za osvobození získal Československou vojenskou pamětní medaili se štítkem Francie. Francouzský Řád čestné legie mu letos v únoru předal francouzský velvyslanec v Česku Stéphane Crouzat. Boje u Dunkerku patřily k významným operacím československých pozemních jednotek na západní frontě za druhé světové války. Československá samostatná obrněná brigáda pod velením generála Aloise Lišky se do obléhání francouzského přístavu zapojila v říjnu 1944. Ve městě bylo tehdy obklíčeno přibližně dvanáct tisíc německých vojáků. Úkolem československé brigády bylo zabránit německé posádce v prolomení obklíčení. Boje pokračovaly až do 9. května 1945, kdy německá posádka kapitulovala. S mobilní aplikací máte ČT24 vždy po ruce. Sledujte živé přenosy, články a krátké zprávy kdekoliv a kdykoliv. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: A security camera view shows an explosion in the distance after an unknown object fell near the Ukrainian border, in Aleksandrów, Poland. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters View image in fullscreen A security camera view shows an explosion in the distance after an unknown object fell near the Ukrainian border, in Aleksandrów, Poland. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters Poland Russian missiles and drone reportedly hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow Jakub Krupa Fri 20 Nov 2026 07.34 EST Last modified on Fri 20 Nov 2026 08.08 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have crashed in Poland during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine. “The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said. Zelenskyy said Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”. The Ukrainian president added: “Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror.” Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, confirmed three violations of Polish airspace, with no injuries reported. He said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”, including the UK. The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises are taking place. Poland’s prime minister called the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia. Donald Tusk said he had spoken with Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte – who will visit Warsaw on Saturday – who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills. “It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said. “Today’s incident shows clearer than ever before why Poland must participate in decisions on Ukraine’s future,” he added, arguing that Warsaw has a “better understanding” of the threat posed by Russia. View image in fullscreen Security personnel secure the area after reports of a possible unidentified object falling in Rudnik nad Sanem, south-eastern Poland. Photograph: Piotr Polak/EPA Rutte said on X: “Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend. “This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.” ​The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who is in Poland for the exercises, described the incursion as “very serious” in a post on X, adding: “The impact of Russia’s illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries. The UK stands in solidarity with our allies.” Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the operational command of the Polish armed forces, said as many as 11 objects had been identified as posing a danger to Polish airspace. He also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the overnight attack on Ukraine, saying Russia used seven bombers and fired 26 Kalibr cruise missiles, 72 Kh-101 cruise missiles and more than 500 drones. Air traffic control at Rzeszów-Jasionka airport – an international passenger hub and major transit point for military aid to Ukraine – was briefly evacuated overnight, for the first time since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine. After the incidents, Tusk summoned army and security service chiefs to an emergency meeting to discuss the situation. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the latest violations “demonstrate the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”. He added: “While Moscow tries to initiate discussions about the ‘new security architecture of Europe’, Russian missiles and drones directly undermine the existing security order in Europe. The first step toward strengthening it would probably be to cease such attacks.” Polish authorities repeatedly warned in recent months against potential security incidents as they feared an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell in Poland’s Lublin region after veering off course during a nightly Russian attack on Ukraine. In September last year, more than 20 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace, with Tusk warning that the country was “closer to military conflict than at any time since the second world war”. In November 2022, a Russian missile Kh-55 crashed near Bydgoszcz, more than 300 miles from Ukraine’s territory, but was only discovered in early 2023. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/27/esto.text: Estonia will close its border with Russia on 1 December, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed in Baku on Friday, stating that “we are not happy about that, but we need to respond and we need to secure Europe as well.”Speaking to reporters at the official opening of the Estonian embassy in Azerbaijan's capital, Tsahkna said his country's decision addresses growing security concerns over Russia’s actions against European countries.He warned that Estonia, which shares a border with Russia, has also faced an increase in Russian sabotage and attacks targeting Europe.Tsahkna travelled to Baku as Estonia increases its diplomatic presence in the South Caucasus, describing his country's new embassy in Baku as a long-term commitment."Every embassy for us has a huge value," he said, while describing the decision to open a diplomatic mission in Azerbaijan as "well calculated"."Our nations, we have a long history together, the same understandings, lots of personal relations, but also the same challenges and interests to the world," Tsahkna said.He added that an intergovernmental commission meeting earlier this month helped move cooperation towards practical projects involving public institutions and private companies.Trading energy and development in the Middle CorridorTsahkna said that Azerbaijan's role in regional and European energy security, as well as the development of the East-West Middle Corridor connecting Asia and Europe, are among Estonia's key interests."We see Azerbaijan as a huge opportunity of learning how you're dealing with energy," the foreign minister said.According to the Estonian foreign minister, the historic peace process and the normalisation between Azerbaijan and Armenia open new perspectives across the South Caucasus, which until recently was dominated by Russia.Estonia also opened an embassy in Armenia earlier this year, demonstrating its strategic interest in boosting its diplomatic presence in both countries and the wider region.Tsahkna outlined Estonia's interest in digitalisation, AI and other technology sectors in Azerbaijan, as well as opportunities emerging from the EU's expanding global trade partnerships.Following a bilateral meeting with Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev, the Estonian foreign minister said that the EU was keen to develop a more practical, long-term cooperation with Azerbaijan, particularly in trade, energy and regional connectivity."Estonia definitely supports the visa liberalisation process between Azerbaijan and the European Union," Tsahkna said.Tourism and education also featured in Tsahkna's address as he called for stronger educational and people-to-people ties, welcoming more Azerbaijani students to Estonia and encouraging greater tourism between the two countries."We are very happy to host your students, your people to Estonia more and more and to see more Estonians as well coming to Azerbaijan," he said.Ukraine remains central to security discussionsTsahkna said he arrived in Baku directly from Kyiv, describing how "the last night I was there, Kyiv was under heavy ballistic missiles attacks," adding that developments in different regions were interconnected.A staunch supporter of Ukraine, Estonia will co-host next year's Ukraine Recovery Conference with the war-torn country.Azerbaijan's assistance has reportedly exceeded $50 million (€45.6 million), and its first humanitarian shipment arrived right after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including food and medicine.In addition, Azerbaijan's State Oil Company (SOCAR) has gas stations across the country providing free fuel for emergency services vehicles.Tsahkna stressed the importance of international assistance to help Ukraine withstand the coming winter, thanking Azerbaijan for the humanitarian support it provides to the war-torn country.From Azerbaijan's perspective, Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov underlined the growing cooperation between the two countries.The opening of Estonia's embassy comes at a time of intense cooperation between the EU and the South Caucasus countries on energy diversification, transport connectivity and regional security.For Tallinn, deeper engagement with Baku is part of a broader effort to strengthen ties with a region increasingly interconnected with Europe's economic and geopolitical priorities.
